news.head: Interim dividend of 3.75 a share, register closes 28 August
news.body: Payment 8 September. Against the 2.25 interim paid in 2024 this is 67% higher. The declaration came before the half-year results, which were still due by 31 August — so the dividend was raised into a profit figure the market had not seen. Three other listed companies raised dividends into falling profit in the same fortnight, so the pattern is worth holding in mind until the number appears.

news.head: Interim dividend of 1.00 a share, register closes 3 September
news.body: Payment 10 September. On a share around 375 that is 0.27%. Car & General is up roughly tenfold in a year; the dividend is not the reason anyone is holding it, and 78% of its profit is a share of Watu Credit, which publishes no accounts.

news.head: Interim dividend of 10.00 a share, register closes 28 August
news.body: Payment 25 September. The biggest per-share payment here, and the reason this counter tops every yield table in the country. Its payout ratio is 134% — it is distributing more than it earns, which is funded by borrowing or by selling something, and cannot continue indefinitely.

news.head: Friday's session was missing from this page until now
news.body: Prices here were stamped Thursday 20 August. A check on 23 August found a Friday 21 August session: Co-operative Bank −6.19% to 36.35, Kenya Power −2.33% to 20.95, KenGen −1.33% to 11.15, Safaricom −0.95% to 36.35, NCBA +0.28% to 90.50. Six counters were updated. For the rest the only source reachable was older than what this page already held, so it was left alone — a price is only replaced by one with a later date on it.

news.head: Five-year profit streak ends — and the dividend goes up 60%
news.body: H1 profit fell 39.8% to KSh 100.4m, revenue −17.2% to KSh 600m, pre-tax −37.4%. Overheads rose 17.3% to KSh 190.8m on fuel and energy. Interim dividend nonetheless raised 60% to KSh 4.00 — the highest in the series. Operating cash flow did improve 40.3% to KSh 236.3m, cash KSh 1.29bn.

news.head: Maiden results: profit +62%, but the engine is Treasury bills
news.body: PAT KSh 3.70bn, H1 EPS 2.23 from 1.75. Net interest income 6.95bn→9.78bn. Loans +10% to 111.06bn; government securities +55% to 94.10bn. Deposits +20% to 180.22bn on flat interest expense. Liquidity ratio 53.1%→61.3%. Due to other banks +198% to 4.54bn. Gross NPLs +19% to 18.14bn. Provisions 663.5m→998.3m. Assets +24% to 238.93bn, equity 33.22bn.

news.head: Record KSh 45.5bn, and the best asset-quality swing of the cycle
news.body: Attributable PAT 43.7bn (+31.5%); group 45.5bn (+32%). Total income +25% to 124.9bn. Assets +20% to 2.16tn. NPL ratio 13.7% → 9.5%. Regional subsidiaries now 52% of banking assets, 42% of PAT. No interim dividend — capital retained for expansion.

news.head: Pre-tax +37% on cheaper funding
news.body: H1 pre-tax 9.84bn. PAT 6.4bn. Total operating income +21% to 26.5bn from 21.9bn. Net interest income +26%. Double-digit loan growth. Reported six days earlier than the estimated date — the share had already run 14% on triple volume.

news.head: 300bn borrowing programme, first 100bn tranche by October
news.body: Five-year medium-term note programme, subject to regulatory approval, alongside a new sustainability bond framework launched at the KCB Leadership Centre. This is debt, not equity — no dilution to shareholders. It signals intent to lend materially more, and it means a KCB bond will shortly exist as a fixed-income alternative.

news.head: Front page calls it speculative retail
news.body: Business Daily attributes the rally to “speculative retail investors”. Market value up from KSh 2.65bn to KSh 27.41bn in twelve months — a 936% increase, about KSh 24.76bn of new paper wealth. The quiet phase is over.

news.head: Profit −17%, dividend raised anyway, no payment date
news.body: Interim dividend lifted to KSh 8.50 from 8.00 while half-year profit fell 17%. Trailing EPS is down 42.19% and the payout ratio stands at 99%. No timeline for the payment was disclosed.

news.head: Profit −10%, dividend +150%, and the parent's buyout failed
news.body: H1 PAT KSh 10.53bn, down from 11.6bn as rate cuts squeezed income. Interim dividend raised 150% to a record KSh 0.50. Net loans a record 329.87bn. Separately the South African parent sought 895.9m shares at KSh 34.50 to reach 85%; only 189.38m came in — a 21.1% take-up. Stake rose to 71.99%, not the 85% intended. Over 64,000 minority holders declined.

news.head: Wider losses, and a plan to open hospitals
news.body: Fuel costs +72%, fleet grounded, intra-Africa routes suspended and frequencies cut. Management's revival strategy is diversification into healthcare, hospitality and education, plus spinning off the maintenance unit.

news.head: Record half-year — on weaker cash
news.body: Revenue +13.1% to KSh 8.38bn, net profit +11.2% to a record KSh 486m, pre-tax +25.5% to 688m, margin 7.4%→8.2%. But net operating cash flow fell 40.9% to 681m and current liabilities rose to 6.05bn from 4.87bn. Assets +19.1% to 10.63bn. KSh 1.56bn now sunk in a loss-making Tanzanian unit. No interim dividend.

news.head: Revenue at a 21-year low
news.body: Broadcasting and digital growth insufficient to offset print collapse; losses widened.

news.head: Foreigners sold in all five sessions while the index rose
news.body: NSE market cap +1.30% to KSh 3.996tn, 3.62bn short of 4 trillion. Banking index +2.83% to 276.63; banks were 55.38% of weekly turnover. Turnover fell 5.62% to 3.92bn and volume fell 25.61% to 100.09m shares. Foreign investors were net sellers of KSh 1.17bn — more than double the prior week — in every session. Locals were 76.2% of turnover.

news.head: Rate held at 8.75% for a fourth straight meeting
news.body: CBK cited stable inflation and exchange rate against elevated global energy risk, and noted declining commercial lending rates supporting private-sector credit. Shilling KSh 129.40/USD, reserves USD 15.25bn, 6.3 months import cover. Three reopened infrastructure bonds drew a record KSh 460.4bn of bids against a KSh 150bn target. T-bills drew 40.8bn against 28bn offered.

legal.title: DPP charges the chief executives of three of the largest banks
legal.body: Charges brought under the Proceeds of Crime and Anti-Money Laundering Act, sections 5 and 44(2). The individuals were charged, not the institutions — a distinction that matters for the shares. But these three banks are roughly a quarter of this exchange's value and all three must publish half-year results within days.
legal.impact: Governance discount and headline risk, not a balance-sheet event. Watch whether any board makes a leadership change before results.

legal.title: Constitutional petition freezes twelve board appointments
legal.body: Governance at the national reinsurer is unresolved by court order until October — arriving in the season when El Niño flood and crop claims land on exactly this balance sheet.
legal.impact: Cannot make major decisions while frozen. Rated Buy, cheap on earnings, and structurally stuck.

legal.title: SIM-swap fraud judgment apportions the bank 40% liability
legal.body: The court apportioned Diamond Trust 40% of the loss, KES 1,788,601. Immaterial as a number against a 47bn market cap.
legal.impact: Precedent, not provision. Establishes bank co-liability in mobile-fraud losses — relevant to every bank with a mobile channel.

legal.title: Moving to take over Kilimani apartments in a 2bn dispute
legal.body: KCB placed the developer Northcote under administration and is moving on the security. Ordinary recovery action for a bank of this size.
legal.impact: Recovery timing, not solvency. Included because it is live and disclosed.

legal.title: Tribunal: KRA cannot deny VAT deductions on supplier red flags alone
legal.body: A taxpayer-favourable ruling limiting the Revenue Authority's ability to disallow input VAT purely because a supplier looks irregular. Relevant to any listed company carrying contested assessments.
legal.impact: Mildly positive across the market for contingent tax liabilities.

legal.title: EPZ firm loses a 390m appeal on burden of proof
legal.body: The company could not prove KRA had received its objection letter. The claim failed on procedure, not merit.
legal.impact: A reminder that tax contingencies in annual reports turn on paperwork, not argument.

legal.title: Parent's tender offer fails to reach its target
legal.body: Absa Group sought 895.9m shares at KSh 34.50 to lift its stake to as much as 85%. Only 189.38m came in. The stake rose to 71.99%, not 85%. Over 64,000 minority holders declined to sell — in a bank whose half-year profit had just fallen 10%.
legal.impact: Free float stays wider than the parent intended. Read the refusal as minority holders expecting more than 34.50 — the share closed at 36.00.

debt.name: KCB Group
debt.head: 300bn note programme, first 100bn tranche by October
debt.body: A five-year medium-term note programme, subject to regulatory approval, launched 19 August alongside a new sustainability bond framework.
debt.read: This is debt, not shares. Nobody's slice of KCB gets smaller — there is no dilution. It signals intent to lend materially more, and it means a KCB bond will exist by October as a fixed-income alternative.

debt.name: Family Bank
debt.head: Interbank borrowing up 198% to 4.54bn
debt.body: Balances due to other banks rose 198% to KSh 4.54bn. Government securities holdings 94.10bn against net loans of 111.06bn. Equity 33.22bn on assets of 238.93bn.
debt.read: Borrowing in the interbank market to fund a Treasury-bill carry trade. It works while rates hold and reverses when they fall — which is precisely what cut Absa's profit 10% this half.

debt.name: Crown Paints
debt.head: Current liabilities 6.05bn while cash conversion fell 41%
debt.body: Current liabilities rose to KSh 6.05bn from 4.87bn in the same half that operating cash flow fell 40.9% to 681m. KSh 1.56bn cumulative sunk into a loss-making Tanzanian subsidiary, 791.47m of it in 2025. Planned capex 141.24m at Lukenya.
debt.read: Rising short-term obligations against falling cash conversion is the combination that ends small manufacturers. Record profit does not offset it.

debt.name: Absa Bank Kenya
debt.head: Record loan book of 329.87bn, and profit still fell
debt.body: Net loans and advances reached a record KSh 329.87bn, up 8%, while half-year profit fell 10% to 10.53bn as rate cuts compressed margin.
debt.read: Growing the book into a falling-rate environment did not protect earnings. That is the read-across to every bank still to report.

debt.name: Sanlam Kenya
debt.head: Borrowings cut to 1.44bn from 4.37bn
debt.body: Borrowings down to KSh 1.44bn from 4.37bn at June 2024. Solvency ratio 266%. But pre-tax profit fell 28.1%, the insurance service result 34.5%, and investment returns 83.3%.
debt.read: The balance sheet was repaired. The earnings engine was not. Deleveraging is not a thesis on its own.

debt.name: Equity Group
debt.head: Assets 2.16 trillion, bad loans 13.7% to 9.5%
debt.body: Total assets expanded 20% to KSh 2.16tn. The non-performing loan ratio fell from 13.7% to 9.5%. Regional subsidiaries are now 52% of banking assets and 42% of profit.
debt.read: The best asset-quality improvement of this cycle. On a balance sheet this size, a 4.2-point NPL fall is worth more than any dividend on this exchange.

debt.name: Kenya Airways
debt.head: Fuel costs up 72%, fleet grounded
debt.body: Fuel costs rose 72%. Aircraft grounded, intra-Africa routes suspended, frequencies cut. Losing KSh 120.31 per share.
debt.read: No debt disclosure changes this picture. The stated revival plan is diversification into hospitals, hotels and education.

debt.name: BOC Kenya
debt.head: Cash flow rose 40% while profit fell 40%
debt.body: Operating cash flow improved 40.3% to KSh 236.3m and cash reserves reached 1.29bn — in the half where net profit fell 39.8% to 100.4m and a five-year growth streak ended.
debt.read: The rare inverse of the Crown Paints problem: worse profit, better cash. Of the two, better cash is the one you want.

income.one: You want money arriving in your account.
income.mean: Twice a year most listed companies send cash to shareholders. That is a dividend. It lands in your bank account and you can spend it. This goal is about getting paid, not about getting rich.
income.accept: The share price may go nowhere for years. You are buying a cheque, not a rocket.
income.kills: A dividend that is not covered by profit. If a company earns 10 and pays out 13, it is borrowing or selling something to pay you. That gets cut — usually without warning. Three companies on this exchange did exactly this in the last week.
income.test: Payout ratio under 90%, and the after-tax yield beating what the government pays you risk-free.

growth.one: You want the price higher than you paid.
growth.mean: You buy at 90, you hope to sell at 140. Dividends are a bonus you barely notice. All of your return comes from someone later paying more than you did.
growth.accept: No cash for years, and the real possibility of being wrong for a long time while holding.
growth.kills: Buying growth that already happened. A share up 400% has already been discovered. And profit that will not repeat — a currency gain, a one-off sale, a share of a company that publishes no accounts.
growth.test: Earnings actually growing, at a price that has not already priced it in, and profit that repeats.

safety.one: You want your money back, plus a bit.
safety.mean: You would rather make 8% you can rely on than 40% you might. You are protecting what you have more than you are building.
safety.accept: You will watch other people make more than you, and it will be uncomfortable.
safety.kills: Buying something you cannot sell. A share nobody trades has a price on the screen and no buyer when you need one. And a dividend funded by borrowing rather than profit.
safety.test: Covered dividend, real daily trading, price not already stretched, and income that at least keeps pace with inflation.

preserve.t: I cannot afford to lose it
preserve.one: This is money you actually need.
preserve.mean: Rent. School fees. The money that stands between you and a crisis. If it halved, something in your life would break.
preserve.accept: Nothing. That is the point. This goal does not accept losses.
preserve.kills: The stock market itself. Any share can fall 30% in a month for reasons that have nothing to do with the company. There is no share on this exchange that is safe in the way this goal needs.
preserve.test: This page will not recommend a share for this goal. It will show you where the money should go instead, and the numbers for that.

edu.s: If it says 6, the company earns back what you paid in about six years at today's rate of profit.
edu.l: Lower looks cheaper. But cheap often means the market expects that profit to fall — so a very low number is a question, not a bargain. Kenya Power sits at 1.65 on this exchange, and that is a warning rather than a gift, because its profit comes from currency movements on dollar debt rather than from selling electricity.

edu.s: Of all the profit the company made, this is the slice sitting behind one share.
edu.l: If a company earns 14.50 per share and the share costs 90, you are paying about 6.2 years of profit. Watch for the word attributable — group profit includes slices belonging to partners in other countries, and that part is not yours.

edu.s: Cash the company sends you, shown as a percentage of what the share costs today.
edu.l: A 7.78% dividend on a 90-shilling share means about 7 shillings a year per share. It is paid in cash, usually twice a year, and it is the only return that does not depend on someone else buying your shares later.

edu.s: Of every 100 shillings the company earns, how much it hands to shareholders.
edu.l: Under 70 is comfortable. Over 100 means it is paying out more than it earns — funded by borrowing or by selling something — and that cannot continue. BAT on this exchange pays 134%. Standard Chartered pays 99% with earnings down 42%. Those are the two highest yields here and both are countdowns.

edu.s: Kenya takes 5% of share dividends and 15% of interest on government paper.
edu.l: This changes which option actually wins, and almost nobody adjusts for it. A 7.96% dividend nets 7.56%. A 9.037% Treasury bill nets 7.68%. The share looks higher and is actually lower. Infrastructure bonds are exempt entirely, which is why they get three times oversubscribed.

edu.s: The government will pay you 9.037% to lend it money for a year, with no risk of the company failing.
edu.l: After its 15% tax that is 7.68%. This is the bar. If a share pays you less than 7.68% in dividends, you are taking company risk for free — the only reason left to own it is a belief the price will rise. Every yield on this page is measured against this line.

edu.s: Prices in Kenya rose 6.49% in the year to July. Your return has to beat that before you are actually ahead.
edu.l: A savings account paying 3.32% loses you 3.17% a year in what your money can buy. You feel richer and get poorer. Every income figure on this page is also shown after inflation, because that is the only version that is true.

edu.s: The price on the screen only exists for the number of shares people are actually trading.
edu.l: This is the one beginners never hear about and it costs the most. If your order is larger than a day's trading, you push the price up against yourself and pay more than the screen says. When you sell, the same in reverse — and there may be nobody there. Of 57 counters here, most cannot absorb even a modest order. Enter your amount above and the page marks which ones can.

edu.s: How hard the price has run recently. Above 70 means the crowd already arrived.
edu.l: It does not mean the price will fall. It means you are not early, and the easy part is behind you. Right now eleven counters here are overbought and none are oversold — there is nowhere on this exchange you can buy something the crowd has abandoned.

edu.s: Profit can come from selling things, or from a one-off that will not happen again.
edu.l: A currency gain on dollar debt. A property revaluation. A share of another company's profit. The first kind repeats and is worth paying for; the others are not. Car & General looks cheap on forward earnings, but 78% of its profit is a share of Watu Credit, which publishes no accounts and whose own profit fell 85% in the 2024 floods.

edu.s: Whether the profit on paper actually turned into money in the bank.
edu.l: Always put these two next to each other. Crown Paints just posted a record half-year profit while its operating cash flow fell 40.9% — the sales are real but the money has not arrived. That gap is the single most useful check an ordinary investor can make, and it takes one minute.

edu.s: The deadline to own a share if you want its next dividend.
edu.l: You must be on the register before that date. And a trade takes three working days to settle, so the last realistic day to buy is roughly three working days earlier. Miss it by a day and you wait a year.

edu.s: Every ratio on every screen is backward-looking. News is what changes the price.
edu.l: This is the lesson that cost the most. A screen showed a share at 12 years of profit while its results, published the day before, had tripled the profit — making it 5.8 years. The ratio was not wrong, it was late. On this page every counter's verdict states what the news does to the numbers, because the numbers alone would have told you to walk past it.

EQTY.t: The news makes this better than the ratios say
EQTY.b: Reported 19 August: profit to shareholders 43.7bn, up 31.5%, and bad loans fell from 13.7% to 9.5%. On a 2.16 trillion balance sheet a 4.2-point fall in bad loans is worth more than any dividend on this exchange. Annualise the half-year and you are paying about 4.0 years of profit, not the 4.72 the trailing screen shows.
EQTY.c: But there is no interim dividend — the cash is being kept for expansion — and the share is overbought after a 5% week. You are buying the better bank at a stretched price with no cash until next year.

DTK.b: Reported 19 August: pre-tax profit +37% to 9.84bn, interest income +26%, total income +21%. It reported six days earlier than the estimated date — which is why the share ran 14% the week before on triple normal volume. Somebody knew.
DTK.c: The figure is the group. Diamond Trust has real minority partners in Tanzania, Uganda and Burundi, so the slice belonging to you is smaller than the headline. And the news is now in the price — momentum 83.8.

SCBK.b: Reported 18 August: profit −17%. Trailing earnings per share are down 42%. It pays out 99% of what it earns — and raised the interim dividend to 8.50 anyway, with no payment date disclosed.
SCBK.c: That 9.00% is the highest apparently-safe income on this exchange and the least safe number on this page. The share fell 5.5% on the day. A screen sorting by yield puts this near the top. Do not let it.

ABSA.b: Reported 18 August: profit fell 10% to 10.53bn as rate cuts squeezed income — and the share rose 4% into overbought territory two days later. It raised the interim dividend 150% to a record 0.50 anyway.
ABSA.c: Separately the South African parent tried to buy 895.9m shares at 34.50 to reach 85%. Only 21.1% came in; the stake went to 71.99%. Over 64,000 small holders refused cash in a bank whose profit is falling. Read that as the crowd expecting more, not as a valuation.

BOC.t: The news ends a five-year story
BOC.b: Reported 21 August: profit −39.8% to 100.4m, revenue −17.2%, and a five-year run of first-half profit growth ended. Overheads rose 17.3% on fuel and energy. The interim dividend was still raised 60% to 4.00 — the third company in one week to do that.
BOC.c: One genuine positive: operating cash flow rose 40.3% to 236.3m and cash reached 1.29bn. Worse profit, better cash — of the two, better cash is the one you want. But the payout is now 80% of a shrinking number.

F.t: The news explains where the growth came from, and it is not banking
F.b: Reported 20 August: profit +62% to 3.70bn. Then look at the engine. Loans grew 10% while holdings of government securities jumped 55% to 94.10bn. Deposits rose 20% while interest costs stayed flat. It is a leveraged Treasury-bill fund with a banking licence. Non-interest income actually fell.
F.c: And bad loans rose 19% to 18.14bn — 16.3% of its loan book, against Equity's 9.5%. You would pay 1.65 times book for that, with no dividend, to access a trade you can do yourself risk-free. It closed at 33.00, below the 37 it touched.

CGEN.t: The news is now the story, and that is the warning
CGEN.b: Half-year profit 2.60bn, up 309%. On 80.2m shares that annualises to about 5.8 years of profit — not expensive at all. One year: +1,066%. Market value went from 2.65bn to 27.41bn.
CGEN.c: On 19 August the national business paper put it on the front page and attributed the rally to “speculative retail investors”. And 78% of that profit is a share of Watu Credit's earnings — an associate that publishes no accounts, whose own profit collapsed 85% in the 2024 floods. El Niño rains are forecast for October. You cannot audit four-fifths of the profit.

KPLC.t: The cheapest number here is the biggest warning
KPLC.b: It earns 12.76 per share on a 21.45 price — 1.65 years of profit, the cheapest on the exchange. The dividend is covered 11.6 times. Rated Buy, genuinely liquid, not overbought. On paper the best thing here.
KPLC.c: But Kenya Power's profit swings on foreign-exchange gains on its dollar debt, not on selling electricity. When the shilling strengthens it books enormous paper gains straight through the income statement. Same category as Car & General's associate income: real in the accounts, not repeatable. Up 88% in a year. Full-year results land 30 September and could look entirely different.

KCB.t: Overbought before the number, and a new borrowing programme
KCB.b: Launched a 300bn medium-term note programme on 19 August, first tranche 100bn targeted by October. Read this correctly: it is debt, not new shares. Nobody's slice gets smaller. It signals intent to lend materially more.
KCB.c: But it is overbought at 84.8 before it has reported, and it must publish by 31 August. Its chief executive was among three charged by the DPP on 5 August. You would be buying a stretched price ahead of a number you have not seen.

NCBA.b: It drifted down while every other large bank rose. It is the only liquid large bank that is not overbought, its 7.78% dividend is covered 2.1 times, and it trades 30.7m a day. Book closure 28 August.
NCBA.c: It has not reported yet — the figures land by 31 August. Earnings growth is only 8.3%, the weakest of the big banks. And its chief executive was among three charged on 5 August. The dividend also nets 7.39% against a 7.68% Treasury bill, so on income alone you are still behind.

TOTL.b: I called this the overlooked one: 8% dividend, earnings up 46%, not overbought, nobody talking about it.
TOTL.c: The dividend is not covered. Payout is 104% — it pays out more than it earns. That is the same defect as BAT, on a smaller company. And it traded 3m in a day. Withdraw the earlier read.

SBIC.t: The right answer you cannot have
SBIC.b: The only counter on this exchange whose covered dividend beats the Treasury bill after tax — 8.22% net against 7.68%, covered 1.47 times, and not overbought. On the numbers alone it wins outright.
SBIC.c: It traded 7,170 shares. Under 2m shillings in a full day. Enter almost any real amount above and this fails the access gate. The best income on the exchange sits behind a door most people cannot fit through.

CARB.b: Up 25% in days, and 7.74% on the last session alone.
CARB.c: Momentum 95.4 — the most overbought reading on the exchange — on volume 13.3 times normal, with no announcement of any kind. No results, no dividend news, nothing. This is the single most dangerous chart on this page and there is no information behind it.

CRWN.b: Reported 17 August: best half-year on record. Revenue 8.38bn (+13.1%), profit 486m (+11.2%), pre-tax margin up to 8.2%. The recovery runs 37m → 75m → 437m → 486m across four first halves.
CRWN.c: Operating cash flow fell 40.9% to 681m and current liabilities rose to 6.05bn from 4.87bn. Profit up, cash down. It also traded 618,000 shillings, so at most real order sizes it is academic anyway.

KQ.t: The plan is the red flag
KQ.b: Losing 120.31 per share. Fuel costs up 72%, aircraft grounded, intra-Africa routes suspended.
KQ.c: Management's stated revival strategy is to diversify into healthcare, hospitality and education and spin off the maintenance unit. An airline that cannot fly profitably is not fixed by opening a hospital.

KEGN.t: The quiet one that holds up
KEGN.b: Highest covered dividend you can realistically buy — 7.96% gross, covered 1.8 times, rated Buy, not overbought, and 15.4m traded a day. El Niño rains fill the dams, and water is free fuel where diesel is not.
KEGN.c: It sells almost everything to one customer — Kenya Power — which has a history of owing it money. Government holds about 70%. And results are not until 30 October, so you would hold ten weeks blind. Nets 7.56% against a 7.68% Treasury bill.

SCOM.t: The only one your order is invisible in
SCOM.b: Traded 561m in a single day — more than the next two counters combined. Half the market's value. Earnings up 37%, payout 63% and covered, rated Strong buy.
SCOM.c: 15.4 years of profit, and the dividend nets 3.92% — barely half the Treasury bill. You would be buying it for growth and for the ability to get out, not for income.

EABL.c: It carries the only Sell rating on this exchange, and on the last session it traded 256m — 7.8 times normal volume — and fell. Heavy volume on a falling price with a Sell rating is distribution, not accumulation.

SLAM.t: Growing the top line while the profit shrinks
SLAM.b: Premiums up 32%, solvency 266%, borrowings cut to 1.44bn from 4.37bn.
SLAM.c: Pre-tax profit −28.1%, insurance service result −34.5%, investment returns −83.3%, and a 147.5m net financial loss. The balance sheet was repaired. The earnings engine was not.

NMG.b: Broadcasting and digital subscriptions are growing.
NMG.c: Not fast enough. Group revenue is at its lowest level in 21 years as print collapses, and losses widened.

COOP.t: A source conflict you must settle yourself
COOP.b: Earnings up 27%, 6.75 years of profit, and 50m traded a day — genuinely liquid.
COOP.c: The dividend figure disagrees across sources. One implies 2.50 per share (6.44%), another has 3.00 (7.74% here, and 8.12% at Friday's intraday low of 36.95). At 3.00 it clears the Treasury bill; at 2.50 it does not. Check the last dividend notice before you size this. It is also overbought and has not reported yet.

KNRE.b: 5.18 years of profit, rated Buy, and 4.2m traded — cheap on the face of it.
KNRE.c: Earnings are falling 11.6%, a court order has frozen twelve board appointments until 1 October, and a forecast El Niño is about to land flood and crop claims on the national reinsurer. Cheap for reasons.

BAT.t: The biggest yield on the exchange is a countdown
BAT.b: 12.59% gross — nothing else here comes close. Earnings up 17%. Book closure 28 August.
BAT.c: It pays out 134% of what it earns. A dividend above profit is funded by borrowing or by selling something, and it gets cut. The only question is when.

NSE.t: A leveraged bet on the thing that just fell
NSE.b: Earnings up 133%, though off a small base — it earns 1.04 per share.
NSE.c: At 25.6 years of profit it is a leveraged bet on trading volumes — and volumes fell 25.61% last week while turnover fell 5.62%. You would be paying a high multiple for a business whose input is shrinking.

TPSE.t: Cheapest real business here, and unbuyable
TPSE.b: 3.68 years of profit with earnings up 197% — the cheapest genuine business on this exchange.
TPSE.c: It traded 87,000 shillings in a full day. And El Niño rains hit safari tourism in the season it earns most. The valuation is real; the access is not.

KPC.t: Flat since listing, and that is the answer
KPC.b: A 9-shilling share on a 165bn company. It looks cheap because the price is small.
KPC.c: It earns 41 cents a share — 22 years of profit — and has declared no dividend at all. Down 1.09% over twelve months. It has gone nowhere because it was priced fully at listing, not because the market is ignoring it. A low share price is not a low valuation.

UMME.t: The trap that catches every yield screener
UMME.b: 393.65% dividend yield. The highest number on any screen of this market.
UMME.c: It is not income. The Uganda concession is ending and capital is being returned to shareholders — you are being handed back your own money, once. Sort any screen by yield and this appears first. Anyone who acts on it has misunderstood what the number is.

OCH.c: It trades at 140 years of profit, earns six cents a share, and earnings are down 76%. Heavy volume on a company this small and this expensive is being pumped, not discovered.

IMH.t: Rose into overbought on thin volume
IMH.b: 6.66 years of profit, earnings up 19%, dividend 5.23%.
IMH.c: It rose 4.1% on the last session on below-normal volume and is now overbought at 79.6. It has also not reported — figures due by 31 August.

NCBA.note: Declared the day after this page's screener capture, which is why it was missing until now. It is 67% above the 2.25 interim paid in 2024. The half-year results were still due by 31 August when it was declared, so the profit behind it was not public at the time.

BAT.note: The largest single payment on this exchange in shillings per share. Read it against a 134% payout ratio — British American Tobacco is paying out more than it earns, and this page flags it for exactly that reason.

CGEN.note: One shilling on a share that costs about 375. That is 0.27% — a rounding error next to the price move, and a reminder that Car & General's story has nothing to do with income.

nextdivmeta.lede: A dividend yield is a trailing number: it tells you what was paid, not what is coming. These are the payments actually declared, with the dates attached. To receive one you must be on the register by the record date, and a trade takes three working days to settle — so the last realistic day to buy is about three working days earlier.
nextdivmeta.gap: Every other counter on this exchange has no declared payment pending that could be verified. That is not the same as never paying — most pay once a year after full-year results. It means there is no dated cash to point at right now.
